newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Jobs, NAPM top heavy calendar.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Jobs, NAPM top heavy calendar.

text.p: A week after the Federal Reserve's somewhat suprising decision to hold interest rates steady, an unusually heavy calendar of economic data lets Wall Street judge for itself the wisdom or folly of the Fed's choice.

Analysts also noted that market focus has begun to shift to third quarter earnings, particularly after last week's profit warning from AT&T Corp. With earnings season just two weeks away, investors are bracing for other warnings.

However, with Wall Street hotly debating the outlook for interest rates, analysts said evidence that the economy's strong growth continued in September would likely have Wall Street second-guessing the Fed and wondering if the central bank had fallen behind the curve on inflation.

Among the major economic indicators slated for release this week are the closely watched National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index, due Tuesday, and monthly unemployment, wage and non-farm payrolls figures, due Friday.
"The expectation and hope is that both reports will indicate the economy basically moderated in September," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.

Analysts have generally ruled out the possibility the data could push the Fed to move on rates before its November interest rate policy meeting and in fact economists are forecasting Friday's numbers will show tamer job growth.

September non-farm payrolls are expected to rise by 166,000, down sharply from 250,000 in August, while the nation's unemployment rate is expected to edge up to 5.2 percent. Average hourly earnings are seen rising 0.2 percent.
Experts forecast a NAPM index reading of 52.5, roughly flat versus August's 52.6 reading.
Even before the NAPM and jobs data, markets will get reports on personal income and consumption as well as new home sales, all due Monday.
Economists forecast a 0.6 percent rise in personal income and a 0.5 percent rise in personal consumption, with annualized new home sales seen at 744,000.

"What really has been driving the economy is consumer spending and I think you'll get some short-term volatility very quickly if personal spending is higher than expected," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.
"I think that number and the housing number have the potential to move the market as much as anything else," Froehlich said.
For individual stocks, with the market far less stubbornly bullish than a year ago, any sign that earnings growth is slipping is likely to be punished severely, analysts said.
"The worries about 1997 earnings are intensifying," said Johnson. "The reason is that most expect the growth rate for corporate earnings is going to slow in the third quarter."
"We saw last week in dramatic fashion with AT&T is what happens when it looks like 1997 earnings will be lower than 1996," Johnson said.
A wild card clouding the near-term outlook is an extraordinary degree of international uncertainty, analysts said.

"I don't think we've ever had a more diverse set of potential international disasters, between Yeltsin's health, the crisis in Israel and the Iraqi situation," said Froelich, adding, "Of course no one can forecast the outcome of those."
